extracted.intended_audience: students and mathematicians writing written proofs (homework and publications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing clear, precise, and readable written mathematical proofs for homework, papers, or textbooks; covers prose, structure, formulas, notation, and levels of detail. Suitable for novice proof writers and those preparing proofs for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing, know who the reader is and what they already know (e.g., a fellow student in the same class, or readers for publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write as if convincing someone with the same background but who doesn't yet know the proof; adapt level of detail and explanations to homework vs publication contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in paragraph form
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ordinary prose narrative (complete sentences and paragraphs) rather than terse symbolic statements or two-column high-school style proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although you might first construct a proof as terse symbolic steps, the write-up should be paragraph-style prose—easier to read and comprehend for complicated proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper English
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow conventions of grammar, usage, punctuation, and spelling; write complete sentences with correct punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sentence fragments, run-on sentences, dangling modifiers; watch subject-verb agreement and parallel structure; use correct spelling and capitalization; consult a good grammar/usage book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce prose clear enough for the intended audience to understand the truth, correctness, and insight of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide intuitive explanations and state the type of proof at the start when the structure isn't a simple direct proof (e.g., 'we will prove the contrapositive' or 'by induction').

rubrics_metrics.name: Include motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain why definitions are made as they are, why one might expect the theorem to be true, how one was led to the proof, and how the result might be used later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation can appear before a theorem, at the start of a proof, or at transitions within proofs; include it when ideas are complicated or follow an unexpected path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the first person sparingly; prefer 'we'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid routinely using 'I'; use 'we' whenever it can reasonably mean 'the writer and the reader'; use 'I' only when referring explicitly to oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'We will prove the theorem by induction on n.' Use 'I' when describing personal provenance: 'I learned this technique from ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid most abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use informal mathematical abbreviations like 's.t.', 'w.r.t.', 'w.l.o.g.', or 'iff' in formal exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are fine for blackboard/notes but make written text ugly and cryptic; exceptions include standard Latin abbreviations like 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' (use them correctly). Reserve 'iff' for informal notes/blackboard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread (self and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your writing from beginning to end after finishing, and preferably wait a while before proofreading; have someone else read it if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofreading catches many silly mistakes; getting another reader improves detection of unclear passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: State precisely what you are proving
rubrics_metrics.description: Always precede a proof with a precise statement (one or more English sentences) of the theorem being proved (copy, summarize, or paraphrase as appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer paraphrasing into a theorem-style statement rather than copying a command-like problem statement; label the statement clearly (Theorem, Proposition, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Label theorems and results
rubrics_metrics.description: Tag each stated result with an identifying label such as Theorem, Proposition, Corollary, or Lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the label choice to signal role: theorem=important result, proposition=interesting but less central, lemma=technical step, corollary=easy consequence. Use typographic conventions (bold/italics) or underline in handwriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show where proofs begin and end
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin proofs with the word 'Proof' and end them with a distinctive symbol (e.g., a square) or QED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in marking proof boundaries helps reader orientation; QED is traditional but the square symbol is now common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with precision (define terms and quantify symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure every mathematical statement has a precise meaning: define terms, use symbols consistently, and quantify every symbolic name appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'What does it mean?' (make terms/symbols defined before first use) and 'Why is it true?' (justify statements by axiom, theorem, definition, hypothesis, a previous step, or logic). Cite reasons when helpful; sometimes obvious steps may be left unstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include more than just formal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present only a sequence of correct formal statements; intersperse words explaining why steps follow and what you are doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a long sequence of formulas is necessary, add narrative at key points to minimize the work required of the reader to follow the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the right amount of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide level of detail based on audience: work out tedious arguments yourself and include details unless they are obviously fillable by the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you think the argument is tedious, do it in detail first; include enough detail to give the reader the 'Aha!' and, for graded homework, to show the grader you did the work. Emulate clear textbook proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal versus informal parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it easy for the reader to tell which parts of the writing are formal (precise definitions and logical steps) and which are informal (motivation, intuition, sketches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear signaling so readers know whether they are reading a rigorous argument or an explanatory sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use in-line formulas for single symbols and short expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include single symbols and most short formulas directly within paragraphs (in-line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This keeps prose readable; reserve displayed equations for large or especially important formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display large or important formulas and number displayed equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Center large or important formulas on their own lines (displayed); if you will refer to a formula later, it must be displayed and numbered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place equation numbers consistently (left or right margins) and keep formatting uniform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure every formula has a grammatical function in a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas (in-line or displayed) should be part of the sentence structure, functioning as nouns or clauses; formulas cannot stand alone as sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check grammatical correctness by reading sentences aloud; ensure symbols are read naturally in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate displayed formulas appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: If a displayed formula ends a sentence, follow it with a period; likewise include appropriate commas/semicolons if the sentence would have required them in-line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punctuation in displayed equations guides reader comprehension of sentence boundaries and thought completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning sentences with mathematical symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't start paragraph sentences with symbols because symbols cannot be capitalized and it obscures sentence starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite to begin with words (e.g., 'The lines ℓ and m are parallel' instead of 'ℓ and m are parallel'); short bulleted/numeric lists may begin with symbols if clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid two in-line formulas separated only by punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not place two inline formulas next to each other separated only by a comma or punctuation, since they may visually merge into one long formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert a word between them or display the relation: e.g., 'if x = 0, then x^2 > 0' rather than 'if x = 0, x^2 > 0'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relation/operator symbols only to connect formulas, not words
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols like =, >, ≤, ∈, ∩, + should connect mathematical formulas or variables, not replace words in English sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'x > 2' as part of a clause, but do not write 'is >' to replace 'is greater than' in ordinary prose. Prefer writing out logical words rather than logical-symbol shorthand unless in formal symbolic logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute logical-symbol shorthand in English prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using symbols for logical terms (⇒, ⇔, ∴, ∵, ∀, ∃, ∧, ∨, ¬) to replace corresponding English words in ordinary exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These symbols belong in complete symbolic logic formulas; outside logic contexts it's usually clearer to write words like 'if', 'therefore', 'for all', 'there exists', 'and', 'or', 'not', etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format built-up mathematical expressions appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Large expressions such as summations, integrals, matrices, or fractions should be displayed or written compactly so they fit naturally in a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inline small fractions should use slash form (x/(y^2+1)); large or complicated fractions should be displayed with horizontal bars. Small numeric fractions like 1/2 may be inline if typesetting is compact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with chained equalities and transitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Only write multiple equalities/relations like a = b = c when the steps can be proved in the shown order and a transitivity relation legitimately applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relations that are transitive (like <, ≤) may be combined and even mixed if transitivity allows; do not mix relations that do not yield the claimed transitive conclusion. In displayed equations, line up relational symbols vertically for clarity.
